title: Streaks fade, averages hold
question: Why do averages settle down when single results never do?
hook: A casino can lose on one spin and still count on a predictable profit.
idea: Averages from many independent trials head toward the true value, but a small number of trials promises nothing.

beats.prompt: A fair coin lands heads 7 times in its first 10 flips. You keep flipping thousands more. Where should the share of heads head?

choices.label: Toward about one half, since the law applies over many flips
Below one half, so tails can make up for the early heads
choices.feedback: A streak is not immediately balanced by the other outcomes, so tails do not get extra chances.

choices.label: Stay near seven tenths, since this coin looks biased
choices.feedback: A fair coin has a theoretical chance of one half, and the proportion follows that over many flips, not the first few.

beats.explain: The proportion of heads converges to one half as the number of flips grows, and early flips are not corrected later.

beats.prompt: Match each situation to what the law of large numbers predicts.
pairs: Flipping a fair coin many times
The share of heads approaches one half
beats.explain: The law ties averages to true values over many trials, and it can fail for heavy-tailed cases such as the Cauchy distribution.

beats.prompt: Sort each claim into whether the law supports it.
items: Average of many dice rolls nears 3.5
Casino earnings tend toward a set percentage over many spins
Share of heads approaches one half over many flips
A streak of heads is immediately balanced by tails
Ten flips must come out exactly five and five
beats.explain: The law concerns large numbers of observations. A small number need not match the expected value, and streaks are not immediately balanced.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which one?
steps: A fair coin has a one half chance of heads on each flip.
Over a huge number of flips, the share of heads should settle near one half.
So after a long run of heads, tails must come up more often to even things out.
So the more flips there are, the closer the share of heads gets to one half.
beats.explain: There is no principle that a streak will immediately be balanced. The share settles through sheer numbers of flips, not because tails are owed.
